In a category \mathcal {C}, a subobject of c is an isomorphism class of monomorphisms into c.
An object c in a category \mathcal {C} is terminal if there is a unique morphism from any other object into it.

Because terminal objects are unique up to unique isomorphism (as are all universal objects) we often just write \top to refer to the terminal object. Likewise, ! : d \to \top refers to the unique morphism into \top .

Subsets A of a set X may classically be identified with a characteristic map \chi _{A} : X \to \mathsf {bool}. Intuitively, for every x : X, \chi _{A} gives a truth value to the statement "x is in the subset A". In this manner, the domain of the characteristic map, \mathsf {bool}, classifies the subsets of X.
Generalizing over this principle, in a category \mathcal {C} an object \Omega is a subobject classifier if maps into it from some object c likewise uniquely identify a subobject of c.

We can understand \Omega to behave like an object of truth values that are not necessarily boolean valued. A morphism p : c \to \Omega can be thought of like a predicate on c. If c were a set, this would precisely be the characteristic function on it. However, this idea can generalize beyond sets. For instance in the category of graphs, \Omega is a cleverly constructed graph such that any graph homomorphism g \to \Omega into it picks out a unique subgraph of g.

There are always two (suggestively named) disjoint "points" of \Omega , thought of as morphisms out of the [terminal object]{sss-001O} \mathsf {true} , \mathsf {false} : \top \to \Omega . I think if we're being careful, \mathsf {true} may properly be the "subobject classifier" but I always use the term to refer to \Omega itself.

Let c and d be objects in a category \mathcal {C} with two parallel morphisms f , g : c \to d. The equalizer of f and g, if it exists, is the universal object \mathsf {eq} with the following property:
There is a morphism \pi : \mathsf {eq} \to c
\pi \circ f = \pi \circ g

For a fixed, finite alphabet \mathcal {A}, a deterministic automaton can be identified with coalgebras of the functor D(X) = 2 \times X^{\mathcal {A}}.

The final coalgebra encodes all languages, and regular languages are the ones corresponding to finite D-coalgebras. More precisely, a language is regular if it is in the image of the final homomorphism from a finite coalgebra to the coalgebra of all languages.

You may view a D-coalgebra X as a state machine through the lens of Brzozowski derivatives. The boolean flag marks if the initial state of X is accepting or not, and the functions X^{\mathcal {A}} define the transitions labelled by each character from this single state to the initial states of more automata. Gathering all of these up into a single transition system describes a (potentially infinite) deterministic automaton.

The identification between regular languages and finite colagebras arises when the resulting automaton has only finitely many states (up to an appropriate equivalence). Although, it may be unclear what we mean when we count two states as "the same". When building a DFA with Brzozowski derivatives, we characterize each of these coalgebras up to weak equivalence. Thus, we need to decidably check when two of these languages are the same. This is harder to generalize to the context-free case as context-free language equivalence is undecidable.

Deterministic regular expressions are a grammar formalism for defining regular expressions that correspond to deterministic regular languages.
In the spirit of Bruggemann-Klein and Wood and Krishaswami and Yallop, inductively define the deterministic regular expressions in terms of their nullability, first set, and followlast set:
\epsilon , the grammar accepting only the empty string.
\texttt {"}c\texttt {"}, the grammar only accepting the length 1 string comprising the character c for some character c drawn from the alphabet
r \otimes r', the concatenation of r and r' where \neg \mathsf {Null}(r) and \mathsf {FLast}(r) \cap \mathsf {First}(r') = \emptyset
r \oplus r', the disjunction of r and r' where \neg (\mathsf {Null}(r) \land \mathsf {Null}(r')) and \mathsf {First}(r) \cap \mathsf {First}(r') = \emptyset
{r}^{*}, the Kleene star of r where \neg \mathsf {Null}(r) and \mathsf {FLast}(r) \cap \mathsf {First}(r) = \emptyset

In each of the above constructors, the constraints on \mathsf {First}(r) and \mathsf {FLast}(r) remove sources of ambiguity in a regular expressions. They provide a sound guarantee that the resulting regular expression has at most one parse for any string.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Intrinsic Verification of Parsers and Formal Grammar Theory in Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:mainmatter.fr:p:
We present Dependent Lambek Calculus, a domain-specific dependent type theory for verified parsing and formal grammar theory. In Dependent Lambek Calculus, linear types are used as a syntax for formal grammars, and parsers can be written as linear terms. The linear typing restriction provides a form of intrinsic verification that a parser yields only valid parse trees for the input string. We demonstrate the expressivity of this system by showing that the combination of inductive linear types and dependency on non-linear data can be used to encode commonly used grammar formalisms such as regular and context-free grammars as well as traces of various types of automata. Using these encodings, we define parsers for regular expressions using deterministic automata, as well as examples of verified parsers of context-free grammars.
We present a denotational semantics of our type theory that interprets the types as a mathematical notion of formal grammars. Based on this denotational semantics, we have made a prototype implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus using a shallow embedding in the Agda proof assistant. All of our examples parsers have been implemented in this prototype implementation.

fr:title.text: Intrinsic Verification of Parsers and Formal Grammar Theory in Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Intrinsic Verification of Parsers and Formal Grammar Theory in Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:mainmatter.fr:p:
We present Dependent Lambek Calculus, a domain-specific dependent type theory for verified parsing and formal grammar theory. In Dependent Lambek Calculus, linear types are used as a syntax for formal grammars, and parsers can be written as linear terms. The linear typing restriction provides a form of intrinsic verification that a parser yields only valid parse trees for the input string. We demonstrate the expressivity of this system by showing that the combination of inductive linear types and dependency on non-linear data can be used to encode commonly used grammar formalisms such as regular and context-free grammars as well as traces of various types of automata. Using these encodings, we define parsers for regular expressions using deterministic automata, as well as examples of verified parsers of context-free grammars.
We present a denotational semantics of our type theory that interprets the types as a mathematical notion of formal grammars. Based on this denotational semantics, we have made a prototype implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus using a shallow embedding in the Agda proof assistant. All of our examples parsers have been implemented in this prototype implementation.
